questions.prompt: What is the average-case time to search for a key in a balanced binary search tree with n nodes?
questions.explanation: A balanced tree keeps its height at O(log n), and each comparison discards one subtree. An unbalanced tree can degrade this to O(n).

questions.prompt: An in-order traversal of a binary search tree visits the keys in what order?
questions.explanation: Visiting left subtree, then node, then right subtree yields keys in increasing order because of the BST ordering property. This is a common way to test whether a tree is a valid BST.

questions.prompt: What is the height of a degenerate (completely skewed) binary search tree with n nodes?
questions.explanation: Inserting already-sorted keys makes each node have a single child, so the tree becomes a linked list of height n - 1. All operations then cost O(n), which is what self-balancing trees prevent.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a full and a complete binary tree?

options.text: A full tree must be balanced; a complete tree need not be
A full tree's nodes have 0 or 2 children; a complete tree fills every level except possibly the last, filled left to right
A complete tree's nodes have 0 or 2 children; a full tree fills levels left to right

questions.explanation: Fullness constrains child count: every node has zero or two children. Completeness constrains shape: all levels packed except the last, which fills from the left. A heap is a complete binary tree.

questions.prompt: Which traversal of a binary tree uses a queue?
questions.explanation: Level-order dequeues a node and enqueues its children, processing the tree level by level. The depth-first traversals use a stack, explicitly or via recursion.

questions.prompt: In a binary search tree, the in-order successor of a node that has a right subtree is:

options.text: The leftmost node of its right subtree
The rightmost node of its left subtree

questions.explanation: The successor is the smallest key larger than the node, which is the minimum of its right subtree, reached by going right once, then left as far as possible.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h (root at height 0)?
questions.explanation: Level i holds at most 2^i nodes, so a tree of height h holds at most 2^0 + 2^1 + ... + 2^h = 2^(h+1) - 1. This maximum is achieved by a perfect binary tree.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time to insert a key into an unbalanced binary search tree?
questions.explanation: Insertion walks down to a leaf position, and in a skewed tree that path has length n. Balanced trees bound this at O(log n) by restructuring after insertion.

questions.prompt: Given the pre-order and in-order traversals of a binary tree with distinct keys, what can be said about the tree?
questions.explanation: Pre-order identifies the root, and in-order splits the remaining keys into left and right subtrees, applied recursively. Pre-order plus post-order, by contrast, is not always sufficient.

questions.prompt: Why can deep recursion on a skewed binary tree cause a stack overflow?

options.text: Each node stores a copy of the whole tree
The recursion depth equals the tree height, which is O(n) when skewed
The tree cannot fit in memory
Traversal visits each node many times

questions.explanation: A recursive traversal nests one call per level, so a height-n skewed tree needs n stack frames. A balanced tree needs only O(log n), which is why balance protects against overflow.
